quantity.description: Change in own-team expected single-game scoring margin from adopting the strategy
quantity.support: unbounded real; positive favors own team

prior.consistency_check: Mode 0.85 lies inside [-0.20, 2.10]; skew-normal support is all of R, covering negative (backfire) effects.

distribution_family.justification: The downside is bounded by the fact that model-recommended gambles are only mildly better than the alternative in most spots, while a strong short-yardage offense could make the payoff substantially larger, so the upside tail is longer.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fit numerically. For standardized skew-normal with alpha=1.2: mode_z = 0.531, 2.5% quantile_z = -0.90, 97.5% quantile_z = 2.238 (alpha=1 has closed form F(z)=Phi(z)^2 giving z-quantiles -1.003/2.239; alpha=1.2 interpolated). Target interval width 2.10-(-0.20)=2.30, so omega = 2.30/3.138 = 0.733; xi = 0.85 - 0.733*0.531 = 0.461. Back-check: xi+omega*(-0.90) = -0.20, xi+omega*2.238 = 2.10.

strategies.rationale: Published WP models show teams still punt or kick in thousands of situations per season where going for it is worth 1-4% win probability each; harvesting those spots is the cheapest available edge and compounds across a full season without requiring any new personnel.
strategies.recommendation: Follow a win-probability-based 4th-down model on essentially every decision, including going for it on 4th-and-short between our own 35 and the opponent's 40, and kicking far fewer long field goals inside the opponent's 35 on 4th-and-medium. Pre-commit in the week's game plan so the decision is made before the play clock starts.
strategies.title: Full 4th-down bot compliance, including own territory

prior.consistency_check: Mode/median 1.15 lies inside [-0.35, 2.70]; Student-t support is unbounded on both sides, allowing a negative effect.

distribution_family.justification: The central estimate is well supported, but the true effect depends heavily on my quarterback, pass protection, and how defenses adapt, so a surprisingly large positive or negative realization is plausible.
distribution_family.name: student_t

strategies.rationale: Public EPA data consistently shows early-down passes outgain early-down runs by a wide margin, and play-action carries a large yards-per-attempt and EPA premium that is empirically uncorrelated with actual run-game success; more efficient early downs mean more manageable third downs, more drives, and more points.
strategies.recommendation: Raise 1st-and-10 dropback rate in the first three quarters toward 60-65% and attach play-action to roughly 35-40% of dropbacks regardless of down, distance, or whether the run game is 'working.' Keep tempo neutral so defenses stay in base personnel against pass concepts.
strategies.title: Early-down pass-first with heavy play-action

prior.consistency_check: Mode 0.45 lies inside [-0.85, 1.75]; normal support is unbounded and signed.

distribution_family.justification: My belief is roughly symmetric around a modest positive effect, and the strategy's dependence on having four rushers who can win alone caps both the upside and downside at moderate magnitudes.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: EPA-per-play data show that opponent rushing efficiency is far less predictive of scoring than explosive passing, and that blitzes that fail produce enormous negative EPA; eliminating explosives and forcing long, mistake-prone drives lowers opponent points more than stuffing runs does.
strategies.recommendation: Default to two-high split-safety structures with a six-man box on early downs, deliberately conceding 4-yard runs, and generate pressure with four-man simulated pressures and stunts instead of five- and six-man blitzes outside of clear passing downs. Blitz volume drops to roughly the bottom quartile of the league.
strategies.title: Light boxes and split-safety early downs, four-man simulated pressure

prior.consistency_check: Mode/median 0.22 lies inside [-0.65, 1.10]; Student-t support is unbounded and signed. Honest note: this is my weakest recommendation and the interval covers zero comfortably.

distribution_family.justification: This is a genuinely weak, evidence-thin pick with a plausibly near-zero effect, but if it prevents a handful of catastrophic pre-snap situations per season the effect could be larger than I expect in either direction.
distribution_family.name: student_t

strategies.rationale: Public analytics prices timeouts almost entirely through end-of-half clock value and is essentially silent on their option value as error-correction tools; my judgment is that a wasted 3rd-down snap out of the wrong personnel costs more expected points than the marginal clock value of a hoarded first-half timeout, though I cannot point to a published model that says so.
strategies.recommendation: Treat first-half timeouts as near-free and call them immediately to prevent a delay of game, fix a badly matched personnel grouping, or stop a defensive substitution disaster, rather than hoarding them for a two-minute drive that may never materialize. Aim to use at least one first-half timeout per game on non-clock grounds.
strategies.title: Spend first-half timeouts as operational assets

prior.consistency_check: Mode 0.28 lies inside [-0.70, 1.60]; skew-normal support is all of R, so a negative effect is representable.

distribution_family.justification: The floor is close to zero because worst case it is just normal play-calling with more preparation, while a well-fit halftime script against an exposed tendency can occasionally be worth a full extra scoring drive, giving a longer upside tail.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fit numerically. For standardized skew-normal with alpha=1.6: mode_z = 0.544, 2.5% quantile_z = -0.72, 97.5% quantile_z = 2.235 (interpolated from the alpha=1 closed form F(z)=Phi(z)^2 and alpha=2.2 Owen's-T evaluation). Target width 1.60-(-0.70)=2.30, so omega = 2.30/2.955 = 0.778; xi = 0.28 - 0.778*0.544 = -0.143. Back-check: xi+omega*(-0.72) = -0.70, xi+omega*2.235 = 1.60.

strategies.rationale: Public analytics documents the value of opening scripts only indirectly and says nothing about second-half or post-turnover scripting; my judgment is that these are the two highest-leverage, most emotionally volatile drives in a game and that removing improvisation from them converts momentum swings into actual points.
strategies.recommendation: Build and rehearse a dedicated 8-12 play script for the first possession of the second half, written at halftime off observed defensive tendencies, plus a pre-built 5-play 'sudden change' script deployed immediately after every takeaway. The quarterback and coordinator rehearse both in Saturday walkthroughs.
strategies.title: Second opening script for the second half and post-turnover drives

prior.consistency_check: Mode/median 0.24 lies inside [-0.80, 1.30]; Student-t support is unbounded and signed, and the heavy tails honestly reflect that this rests on judgment rather than published evidence.

distribution_family.justification: The downside is real if my backups are far worse than my starters, and the upside is real if late-game pressure is as decisive as I suspect, so I want heavy tails around a modest center.
distribution_family.name: student_t

strategies.rationale: Public analytics on pass-rush fatigue is essentially nonexistent because snap-level conditioning data is not public and rotation is confounded with talent gaps; my judgment from watching fourth-quarter protection breakdowns is that pressure rate late in games is worth more than the marginal snaps a tired starter takes in the second quarter.
strategies.recommendation: Impose a strict in-game snap ceiling (roughly 42-46 defensive snaps) on each edge rusher and interior rusher through three quarters, rotating a genuine four-man second wave even when the starters are producing, so the closing unit is fresh for the fourth quarter. Rotations are scheduled by series, not by feel.
strategies.title: Hard snap-count caps on pass rushers to bank fourth-quarter freshness
